name: Microabrasion

angle.text: Users look to microabrasion to clear white or brown spots, including fluorosis marks, so front teeth look more even in colour. The surface change is visible right after a dentist polishes the tooth, and the method has been in clinical use since the 1980s.

summary: A dentist-applied acid-pumice polish that removes a sliver of stained enamel; used for fluorosis and white spots.
note: Removes enamel permanently and is unsuited to dentine staining such as tetracycline.
currentQuick:
Microabrasion removes a very thin layer of surface enamel with a mild acid and pumice to lessen stains and white spots. It dates to a 1986 method by Croll and Cavanaugh.
It is mainly used for mild to moderate fluorosis and enamel defects.
How it works: Combined chemical and mechanical action takes away a few tenths of a millimetre of enamel, removing superficial discolouration.
Risks and caveats: Enamel removed does not regrow, and thinning can expose darker dentine. It does not treat stains deep in dentine.
deepLead:
Enamel microabrasion is a cosmetic dental procedure that removes a very thin outer layer of enamel, using a mildly acidic abrasive compound, to reduce surface discolouration such as white or brown spots. The first practical method, using weak hydrochloric acid and pumice, was developed by Theodore Croll and Richard Cavanaugh in 1986.
It is used mainly for dental fluorosis and for enamel defects including white spot lesions after orthodontic appliances. It is not suited to discolouration located in dentine, such as tetracycline staining.
Several recent clinical trials, registered mostly from 2019 onward, compare microabrasion with resin infiltration and other minimally invasive options.

name: Resin infiltration (ICON)

angle.text: Resin infiltration such as Icon is used to mask white spot lesions left by braces or early decay without drilling, so the tooth surface matches the surrounding enamel. The colour blending is visible after treatment, and many trials exist on its effect on lesion progression.

summary: A resin that seeps into white spots to arrest early lesions and blend them in; trials are many, outcomes not summarised here.
note: Used by dentists; long-term cosmetic outcome data were not found in the sources reviewed.
currentQuick:
Resin infiltration fills the porous enamel of early lesions with a thin resin. Dentists use it for white spots after braces and some fluorosis or hypomineralisation marks.
It has randomised trials and many registered studies behind it.
How it works: Low-viscosity resin penetrates demineralised enamel, stabilising it and changing its light scattering so spots look closer to surrounding enamel.
Risks and caveats: The sources reviewed do not list specific harms. Long-term cosmetic results were not summarised, and one registered fluorosis follow-up was withdrawn.
deepLead:
Resin infiltration is a micro-invasive dental treatment in which a low-viscosity resin is infiltrated into porous, demineralised enamel to arrest early lesions and, as a cosmetic effect, mask white spots; Icon is the best-known commercial product. An encyclopedia article on tooth decay describes resin infiltration as a micro-invasive intervention shown to slow progression of proximal decay.
In appearance contexts it is discussed for white spot lesions after braces and for opacities from fluorosis or molar incisor hypomineralisation. Published case reports and randomised trials exist, and many trials are registered.

name: Whitening LED tray with red light

angle.text: At-home users buy LED trays with red light hoping to speed up peroxide gel whitening for a brighter smile. The gel does the bleaching; the claim that red light adds to it is a marketing premise, and trials of light in general bleaching are mixed with no red-specific data.

summary: A mouth tray with LED and red light sold to boost at-home whitening gel; light benefit in general bleaching is mixed and red-specific data is absent.
note: Results come mainly from the gel; sensitivity and gum irritation are the common side effects.
currentQuick:
These trays combine a whitening gel with LED lights, some red, and are sold for home use. The light is marketed as speeding up whitening.
Research on light in professional bleaching is mixed, and no trial of red-light trays specifically was found.
How it works: The gel's peroxide breaks down stain molecules. The light is claimed to accelerate this, though reviews of light activation disagree on whether it adds benefit and note possible heating.
Risks and caveats: Tooth sensitivity and gum irritation are the commonly reported effects. Whitening results can fade within months, and peroxide limits differ by country.
deepLead:
A whitening LED tray with red light is a consumer device that combines a mouth tray, usually loaded with a peroxide-based or other whitening gel, with built-in light-emitting diodes, some of which emit red light, marketed for at-home tooth whitening. The light component is sold as a way to speed up or enhance the action of the gel.
Tooth whitening generally works by breaking down pigment molecules with peroxide, and in-office systems have long paired gels with halogen, LED or plasma-arc lights . Published reviews of that light-activation practice have reported mixed results: one meta-analysis found light could help when used properly, while a later study found no improvement and noted possible heating of tissue . No published clinical trial specific to red-light LED trays was located for this article.

name: Blue-light teeth whitening device

angle.text: Consumers use blue-light gadgets, with or without gel, to get whiter teeth at home. The idea comes from in-office light-accelerated bleaching, where some studies show light as an add-on to peroxide; light on its own has little data.

summary: LED gadgets sold to whiten teeth with blue light; light helps only as an add-on to peroxide in some studies, and light-only data is lacking.
note: No studies of light-only whitening were found.
currentQuick:
Blue-light whitening devices are consumer LED gadgets, some sold to whiten with light alone.
Dentistry uses light with peroxide gel, and reviews of that practice are mixed. No evidence for light-only whitening was found.
How it works: Whitening is attributed to peroxide breaking down stain molecules. Light is proposed to speed this, though its benefit is debated.
Risks and caveats: Sensitivity and gum irritation are common with peroxide whitening; light may add heat. Results can fade within months.
deepLead:
A blue-light teeth whitening device is a consumer gadget, often a handheld or mouthpiece LED unit, marketed to whiten teeth with light, sometimes with a gel and sometimes on its own. The category is tied to light-accelerated (power) bleaching in dental offices, which uses halogen, LED or plasma lights together with high-concentration peroxide gel .
Whitening chemistry is attributed to peroxide breaking down pigment molecules . Reviews of adding light to peroxide bleaching have reached mixed conclusions, and no sources reviewed for this article describe a clinical trial showing whitening by blue light alone.

name: Electric toothbrush whitening heads

angle.text: Users swap in whitening heads on powered brushes to lift coffee, tea and other surface stain for a brighter smile. Polishing cups and pads are designed for stain removal, though no trials of these specific heads were found.

summary: Polishing-style replacement heads for powered brushes; they can address surface stain, with no head-specific trials found.
note: Does not change intrinsic tooth colour.
currentQuick:
Whitening heads are replacement heads for electric toothbrushes, sold to lift surface stains.
No studies of the heads themselves were found; electric brushes overall show modest plaque benefits.
How it works: Polishing bristles or pads mechanically remove surface stain. They do not bleach internal tooth colour.
Risks and caveats: Heavy brushing pressure can harm enamel and gums. Heads are advised to be replaced about every three months.
deepLead:
Electric toothbrush whitening heads are replacement brush heads marketed for use with powered toothbrushes to remove surface stains and make teeth look whiter. They typically differ from standard heads in bristle layout or a polishing cup or pad.
Electric toothbrushes in general are described as removing more plaque and reducing gum inflammation than manual brushes in a 2014 Cochrane review, though the review's authors questioned the clinical importance of the difference . Mechanical brushing mainly addresses surface (extrinsic) stains; it does not bleach the tooth interior .

name: Teeth whitening Hollywood smile Turkey trip

angle.text: People travel to Turkey for a veneer-and-whitening makeover that delivers a bright, uniform smile at lower prices than in Western Europe. The new look is visible once the work is fitted, and forum and clinical discussion centres on enamel removal and aftercare.

summary: Travelling to Turkey for a veneer-and-whitening smile makeover at lower prices; documented concerns centre on enamel removal and aftercare.
note: Veneer prep can remove enamel; follow-up care may be hard from abroad.
currentQuick:
People travel to Turkey for cosmetic smile makeovers, usually veneers or crowns plus whitening, attracted by lower prices.
No studies of these trips specifically were found.
How it works: Porcelain or composite veneers are bonded over reshaped teeth, and whitening uses peroxide gel.
Risks and caveats: Tooth preparation can remove enamel and cause sensitivity or decay. Aftercare and recourse can be limited abroad.
deepLead:
A Hollywood smile Turkey trip is a form of dental tourism in which a person travels to Turkey for a cosmetic smile makeover, commonly involving porcelain veneers or crowns, often combined with whitening. Turkey is described as a notable destination for dental work such as veneers, crowns and implants in cities including Istanbul, Ankara and Antalya, with costs considerably lower than in Western Europe .
Dental veneers are thin shells of porcelain or composite bonded to teeth; preparation can involve removing some enamel . Medical tourism in general is associated with reported risks including variable aftercare and difficulty obtaining follow-up treatment at home .

name: Metal braces

angle.text: Metal braces are the standard route to straight teeth for teens and adults seeking a better smile. Alignment improves gradually over treatment, and the method is well established in orthodontics.

summary: Classic fixed brackets-and-wire orthodontics; well-established for tooth alignment, highly visible.
note: Needs retainers afterward; plaque control matters.
currentQuick:
Metal braces are the standard fixed orthodontic appliance, using bonded steel brackets and a wire to move teeth.
Treatment commonly takes months to a couple of years, followed by retainers.
How it works: Steady pressure from the wire loosens teeth, and bone remodels to support the new position.
Risks and caveats: Plaque buildup, gum inflammation, soreness and some root shortening are reported. They are very visible.
deepLead:
Metal braces are the traditional form of fixed orthodontic appliance: stainless steel brackets bonded to the teeth and joined by an archwire, held with elastic ties or built-in clips (self-ligating) . They apply steady pressure so that bone remodels around moved teeth, and are the most common type of braces .
Treatment usually lasts from about six months to two and a half years, followed by retainers . Research on how others perceive appliances includes laypeople's ratings of attractiveness, acceptability and value of different appliances , and surveys of adult orthodontic patients' motivations .

name: Ceramic braces

angle.text: Ceramic braces are chosen by people who want straighter teeth with less visible hardware during treatment. They use the same bracket-and-wire mechanics as metal braces, so alignment follows the same established path.

summary: Tooth-coloured fixed braces that trade some visibility for the same bracket-and-wire mechanics.
note: Ceramic brackets differ from metal in debonding and enamel-stress laboratory findings.
currentQuick:
Ceramic braces use tooth-coloured brackets with a wire to straighten teeth, aiming to be less visible than metal.
Research is mostly surveys and lab studies.
How it works: Same as other fixed braces: steady wire pressure moves teeth as bone remodels.
Risks and caveats: Fixed appliances raise plaque and Candida colonisation; lab work examines enamel micro-cracks on debonding.
deepLead:
Ceramic braces are fixed orthodontic appliances whose brackets are tooth-coloured rather than metal, designed to be less noticeable than traditional metal braces. They work like other fixed braces, using brackets and an archwire to apply pressure that moves teeth .
Research includes comparisons of microbial adhesion on metal, ceramic and self-ligating brackets in vitro , surveys of how adults weigh aesthetics when choosing appliances , and a study of appliance type and hiring prospects .

name: Direct-to-consumer aligners (SmileDirectClub)

angle.text: Mail-order aligners were promoted to people wanting straighter teeth more cheaply and conveniently than traditional orthodontics. Alignment comes from the aligners moving teeth over months; SmileDirectClub, the best-known brand, went bankrupt in 2023 after professional complaints.

summary: Mail-order clear aligners that promised cheaper straight teeth; the flagship company went bankrupt in 2023 amid professional complaints.
note: Remote-supervised treatment drew complaints from orthodontist groups; SmileDirectClub ceased operations in 2023-24.
currentQuick:
Direct-to-consumer aligners are clear plastic trays ordered online after a home impression kit or a scan at a studio, with a dentist reviewing the case remotely. SmileDirectClub was the biggest name and pitched them as a cheaper, easier route to straighter teeth than braces.
The model drew complaints from orthodontic associations and dental boards, and the company filed for bankruptcy in 2023 and wound down in early 2024. Research located so far is mostly surveys and commentary rather than outcome trials.
How it works: Like other clear aligners, the trays are worn in sequence to move teeth gradually. The difference lies in the service model: the case is assessed from impressions or scans and monitored remotely rather than at in-person visits.
Risks and caveats: The American Association of Orthodontists filed complaints with state dental boards about the company, and a hidden-camera investigation reported that reviewing orthodontists disagreed with approved plans. The company disputed these characterizations. Published commentary in the dental literature describes the model as raising dilemmas for patients and clinicians.
deepLead:
Direct-to-consumer (DTC) aligners are clear plastic orthodontic aligners marketed straight to the public, usually through an online ordering process in which the patient takes dental impressions or scans at home or in a retail studio and a dentist or orthodontist reviews the case remotely. The best-known example was SmileDirectClub, a Nashville-based company founded in 2014 by Jordan Katzman and Alex Fenkell.
The model was promoted as a lower-cost, more convenient alternative to braces and in-office aligners. Professional bodies, notably the American Association of Orthodontists, filed complaints with state dental boards about the company's practices, and a 2024 commentary in the Journal of the American Dental Association discussed the dilemma these products pose for patients and dentists.
SmileDirectClub filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on September 29, 2023, and began liquidating in early 2024; its assets and technology were acquired by another Nashville company, SmileSet. Other DTC aligner brands continue to exist.

name: Self-ligating braces (Damon)

angle.text: Self-ligating braces such as Damon are marketed as a faster, gentler route to straight teeth. Alignment is the established outcome; claims of speed or comfort over conventional brackets have been compared in trial reviews.

summary: Braces whose brackets clip the wire themselves, marketed as faster and gentler; trial reviews have compared them against conventional brackets.
note: Manufacturer claims of speed and comfort are not clearly attributed to trial evidence in encyclopedic sources.
currentQuick:
Self-ligating braces are metal or ceramic brackets with a built-in clip that holds the wire, so no elastic ties are needed. Damon is the best-known system.
Proponents describe shorter treatment, less pain and fewer visits. A network meta-analysis of randomized trials has examined whether efficiency differs from conventional brackets.
How it works: The built-in clip is meant to let the archwire slide with less restriction. Teeth move in response to the wire's force, as with any fixed braces.
Risks and caveats: Risks resemble those of fixed braces generally: plaque build-up and gum inflammation, white spot lesions, some root resorption and discomfort.
deepLead:
Self-ligating braces are fixed orthodontic brackets that hold the archwire with a built-in clip or slide rather than with elastic or wire ties. They are described as the second most common type of braces, and the Damon system is one commercial brand of them.
Manufacturers and some clinicians have said the design lowers friction, shortens treatment, reduces discomfort and requires fewer appointments. Systematic reviews of randomized trials have compared conventional, passive self-ligating and active self-ligating brackets on treatment efficiency.
Evidence available for this entry is limited to a network meta-analysis, a retrospective stability study and laboratory or microbiological work; the entry's appearance relevance is as a type of braces used for tooth alignment.

name: Retainers

angle.text: Retainers keep a smile straight after braces or aligners by holding teeth where they were moved. Looksmaxxing forums also debate whether retainers affect palate or jaw development, a theory that has not been tested.

summary: Plastic or wire appliances that keep teeth where braces put them; forums debate whether they hold back jaw growth, which nobody has tested.
note: Claims that retainers stunt palate growth are untested; wearing instructions come from the treating orthodontist.
currentQuick:
Retainers are worn after braces or aligners to keep teeth from drifting back. Types include Hawley retainers, clear vacuum-formed trays and wires bonded behind the front teeth.
On looksmax.org, some users worry that retainers restrict palate growth or undo mewing. No studies cited here address that.
How it works: They hold teeth in position while the gum fibers and bone adapt to the new arrangement. Fixed bonded wires work continuously; removable ones depend on being worn.
Risks and caveats: Reported problems include decay when clear retainers are worn while eating or drinking sugary fluids, plaque and gum inflammation if not cleaned, speech effects from Hawley designs, breakage and warping.
deepLead:
Orthodontic retainers are appliances worn after braces or aligners to hold teeth in their corrected positions. Teeth can drift back toward their former positions (relapse) because of recoil of gum fibers, soft-tissue pressure, the bite and continued jaw growth.
Common types are Hawley retainers (a wire and acrylic palate plate), vacuum-formed clear retainers, and fixed retainers bonded behind the teeth. How long they are worn is set by the treating orthodontist and may be indefinite.
In looksmaxxing forums, retainers are also discussed in connection with mewing and jaw or palate development, with some users asking whether wearing them could restrict maxillary growth. No studies cited here test that question.

name: Fixed lingual retainer

angle.text: A bonded wire behind the lower front teeth is used to preserve the alignment gained from braces without a removable appliance to remember. It is an established orthodontic retention method, especially where relapse is considered likely.

summary: A wire glued behind the lower front teeth to stop relapse; it stays put, but is harder to clean.
note: Hygiene around the wire matters; bonds can fail.
currentQuick:
A fixed lingual retainer is a small wire bonded behind the front teeth, usually the lower ones, to keep them from shifting after braces.
It works continuously without the patient having to remember to wear it, but cleaning around it is harder. Trials have compared materials and fixed versus removable designs.
How it works: The wire holds adjacent teeth together so they cannot drift back toward their old positions.
Risks and caveats: Plaque and gum inflammation if not cleaned well, and the bond can fail, which is why bonding techniques have been studied.
deepLead:
A fixed lingual retainer is a thin wire bonded to the tongue-side surfaces of the front teeth, most often the lower front teeth, to hold them in position after orthodontic treatment. It is typically bonded to the six front teeth or only the canines, and is used where relapse is considered more likely, such as after correction of severe rotations or gaps.
Because it is not removed, it needs little patient cooperation, but it is harder to clean around than removable retainers. Published work has compared fixed and removable retainers on microbial levels and gum health, tested different wire materials, and examined bond failure.

name: Accelerated orthodontics (AcceleDent / Propel)

chain: Vibration, light or surgery stimulates bone
angle.text: People in braces or aligners look at AcceleDent, light therapy and Propel micro-perforations to shorten treatment time and reach a straight smile sooner. Evidence for the non-surgical options is described as weak, while surgical versions have shown more effect.

summary: Vibration, light, bone-perforation and surgical add-ons that promise shorter braces time; evidence for non-surgical versions is weak, surgical ones more effective but invasive.
note: Surgical versions add procedural risk; non-surgical evidence described as low certainty.
currentQuick:
Accelerated orthodontics covers add-ons to braces or aligners meant to cut treatment time, from daily vibration devices to light therapy, bone micro-perforations and surgery on the jawbone.
Summaries of reviews describe low-certainty evidence for non-surgical methods, while surgical methods may speed movement more but rest on limited high-quality research.
How it works: The goal is to boost bone remodeling around the tooth roots, either with gentle stimulation or by injuring the bone surface to trigger a temporary burst of remodeling.
Risks and caveats: Surgical forms involve pain, swelling and procedural complications; reviews have noted that harms are not always reported transparently in trials.
deepLead:
Accelerated orthodontics refers to adjuncts used with braces or clear aligners that aim to speed tooth movement and shorten treatment. They are commonly grouped as non-surgical methods, such as cyclic vibration devices (AcceleDent is one brand), low-level light therapy and micro-osteoperforations such as the Propel system, and surgical methods such as corticotomy, piezocision and periodontally accelerated osteogenic orthodontics.
Surgical procedures are intended to injure the outer bone layer and trigger a temporary burst of bone remodeling, called the regional acceleratory phenomenon. Systematic reviews have examined these methods and their harms. According to a Grokipedia summary of a 2023 Cochrane review, evidence that non-surgical adjuncts meaningfully shorten overall treatment is of low to very low certainty.

name: Surgically assisted rapid palatal expansion (SARPE)

angle.text: Adults who want a wider upper jaw use SARPE after non-surgical expansion is no longer an option, and forum posters link the widening to a fuller, better-proportioned face. The skeletal widening is established for narrow-jaw bite problems, while the facial-aesthetic benefit is mostly anecdotal.

summary: Jaw surgery plus an expander to widen the upper jaw in adults; established for narrow-jaw bite problems, its facial-aesthetic value is mostly forum lore.
note: Involves bone cuts under general anesthesia; complications are documented.
currentQuick:
SARPE is a surgical-orthodontic procedure that widens the upper jaw in adults whose palate suture has fused. It is used clinically for narrow upper jaws causing crossbite and crowding.
On looksmax.org it is discussed as an adult option to widen the maxilla and face. Clinical literature describes dental and skeletal outcomes rather than facial appearance.
How it works: A surgeon makes bone cuts to reduce the resistance of the maxilla, and an expander cemented to the teeth or anchored to bone is turned gradually while new bone fills the gap.
Risks and caveats: Reviews catalogue complications, and common effects include discomfort, swelling and a gap between the front teeth. The procedure uses general anesthesia and bone cuts, and alternatives include miniscrew-assisted expansion.
deepLead:
Surgically assisted rapid palatal expansion (SARPE), also called SARME, is a combined surgical and orthodontic procedure that widens the upper jaw in people whose midpalatal suture has fused after puberty. A surgeon makes bone cuts to release resistance, after which an expander appliance is gradually activated to widen the maxilla.
It is a recognized treatment for transverse maxillary deficiency, a narrow upper jaw relative to the lower, which can cause posterior crossbite and crowding. In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as an option for widening the upper jaw and face in adults when non-surgical expansion is considered no longer effective.
Non-surgical alternatives, such as miniscrew-assisted expansion (MARPE), have been developed to avoid surgery in some adult patients.

name: MARPE (mini-implant palate expander)

angle.text: Teens and young adults use MARPE to widen the upper jaw without cutting bone, and forum users hope for a broader midface and cheekbone support. Studies show skeletal widening for narrow jaws; cosmetic facial effects are barely studied.

summary: A palate expander anchored to the palatal bone with mini-screws so it can widen the upper jaw in teens and young adults without cutting the bone; studies show skeletal widening, but cosmetic effects are barely studied.
note: Evidence is for transverse maxillary deficiency (bite and airway); effects on facial aesthetics are not well established, and expansion amounts vary with age and suture maturity.
currentQuick:
MARPE is an orthodontic appliance that widens a narrow upper jaw. It resembles a conventional rapid palatal expander, but is fixed to the roof of the mouth with small bone screws instead of relying only on the teeth. This is intended to push the two halves of the palate apart rather than tipping the teeth outward.
In looksmaxxing communities it is treated as a core non-surgical 'hardmaxx' tool for a narrow palate, with users discussing cheekbone width, midface support and breathing. Published research focuses on bite correction and skeletal change on CBCT scans, not on attractiveness.
How it works: Two to four mini-implants engage the palatal bone and the expander screw is turned to separate the midpalatal suture. Because the force is delivered to bone, proponents say more of the change is skeletal, and a meta-analysis and CBCT studies of late adolescents and young adults report skeletal expansion along with some dental change.
Risks and caveats: Reported issues include incomplete suture opening in some patients, tooth tipping, pain, soreness, screw loosening or failure and expansion that is greater at the front of the palate than the back. It is a prescription orthodontic procedure; users on forums report costs in the thousands of dollars. Studies of long-term stability and facial appearance are limited.
deepLead:
MARPE (micro-implant or miniscrew-assisted rapid palatal expansion) is an orthodontic technique for widening the upper jaw in patients whose midpalatal suture is no longer easily opened by a conventional tooth-borne expander. The appliance is anchored to the palate with mini-implants and is used to treat maxillary transverse deficiency, a narrow upper jaw associated with crossbite, crowding and, in some patients, nasal airway restriction .
Clinical reports describe it as a non-surgical option for adults and late adolescents, as an alternative to surgically assisted expansion . A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis examined its efficacy in late adolescents and adults , and a randomized trial compared conventional expansion with MARPE using low-dose CBCT . A named variant, the Maxillary Skeletal Expander (MSE), uses four bicortical mini-implants .
In looksmaxxing culture MARPE is discussed as a way to widen the maxilla and, proponents say, improve midface width and breathing . The published literature addresses skeletal and dental outcomes; a trial of three-dimensional facial soft tissue changes and perceived appearance after MARPE is registered but not yet recruiting .

name: Palate expander

angle.text: Palate expanders are used mainly in children and teens to widen a narrow upper jaw, and looksmaxxing posters hope for a wider, better-looking face as well. Widening for crossbite and narrow palates is well established; effects on facial looks are largely unstudied.

summary: An orthodontic appliance that widens the upper jaw, mainly in children and teens; well established for narrow palates and crossbites, with cosmetic effects on the face largely unstudied.
note: Established for transverse maxillary deficiency; works best before the palatal suture fuses, and adults often need MARPE or surgically assisted expansion instead.
currentQuick:
A palate expander is a fixed orthodontic appliance, usually cemented to the upper molars, with a central screw that is turned to push the two halves of the upper jaw apart. Orthodontists use it for a narrow upper jaw, crossbites and crowding, most commonly between ages 8 and 18.
Looksmaxxing forums discuss it as a way to widen the maxilla and midface and improve breathing, often asking whether it still works at 16 or 17. The evidence base is mostly about dental arch width and bite, not about facial attractiveness.
How it works: Turning the screw gradually separates the midpalatal suture and the bone fills the gap during a retention period of several months. After puberty the suture is more rigid, so expansion shifts toward tipping teeth, which is why adults are often treated with bone-anchored appliances such as MARPE or with surgery.
Risks and caveats: Reported adverse effects include speech changes such as a lisp, extra saliva, pain, headaches, tongue sores, a gap between the upper front teeth and periodontal changes. Some expansion can be lost afterward, according to older studies summarised by Wikipedia. It is prescribed and monitored by an orthodontist.
deepLead:
A palate expander (also called a rapid palatal expander, RPE or RME) is an orthodontic appliance that widens the upper jaw. A screw mechanism, usually anchored to the upper molars, is activated gradually to separate the midpalatal suture and increase maxillary width .
It is mainly used to correct a narrow upper jaw with posterior crossbite, crowding and some airway concerns, and is most common in ages 8 to 18; it is generally believed to work best before or around the pubertal growth spurt . Expanders are also used in cleft lip and palate patients  and in combination with facemask treatment for Class III malocclusion .
In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as a way to widen the midface and palate and to improve breathing . Published studies report dental arch and skeletal changes; no study in the sources reviewed has tested effects on general facial attractiveness.

name: Orthotropics

angle.text: Followers of John Mew's orthotropics, the root of mewing, hold that tongue posture and oral habits shape the jaw and midface during growth, and adopt it for a more defined face. Mainstream orthodontics regards the evidence for that facial effect as inadequate.

summary: John Mew's theory that tongue posture and oral habits shape facial growth, the root of 'mewing'; mainstream orthodontics regards the evidence as inadequate.
note: Evidence for efficacy is described as inadequate by reviewers; a 12-pair twin study exists but is small, and the practice's founder faced regulatory action.
currentQuick:
Orthotropics is an approach to facial growth developed by British orthodontist John Mew, who argued that resting tongue posture, mouth breathing and soft-food diets shape the jaws and face. Its popular offshoot is 'mewing', in which the tongue rests against the roof of the mouth.
It is a major reference point in looksmaxxing communities, where users share guides and plans. Mainstream orthodontists do not regard it as an established alternative to conventional treatment, and published evidence is limited.
How it works: Proponents say the tongue, lips and jaws acting together influence how the facial bones develop, and that treatment can use palate expansion plus postural appliances (Mew's Biobloc system) and posture training. The theory attributes malocclusion largely to environmental rather than genetic causes.
Risks and caveats: Posture exercises are widely discussed as low-risk, but forum users report jaw or joint discomfort. Wikipedia reports that Mike Mew faced a misconduct process in the UK involving harm claims by child patients' families. Orthodontic appliances carry their usual risks.
deepLead:
Orthotropics is a theory and treatment approach founded by British orthodontist John Mew (1928 to 2025), which holds that the resting posture and function of the tongue, lips and jaws influence facial growth and that malocclusion is largely environmental . Mew framed this as the 'tropic premise' in 1958 .
The approach has been popularised online as 'mewing', named by his son, orthodontist Mike Mew; media attention rose around 2019 . Treatment can include palate expansion followed by a postural appliance, in Mew's Biobloc system .
Mainstream orthodontic organisations and reviewers say evidence for orthotropics is inadequate and that it is not a viable alternative to orthognathic surgery . A small study of 12 pairs of identical twins treated with either orthotropics or fixed appliances is among the few published comparisons .

name: Facial growth guidance appliances (Biobloc / Twin Block)

angle.text: Parents and orthotropics followers use growth guidance appliances in children to steer jaw development toward a better-balanced face. Twin Block is a mainstream functional appliance, while Biobloc belongs to the orthotropics camp, and evidence for its facial effects is limited.

summary: Removable or fixed orthodontic appliances meant to steer jaw growth in children; Biobloc belongs to the orthotropics camp, and evidence for its facial effects is limited.
note: Thin source base; Biobloc is tied to orthotropics, whose efficacy reviewers describe as inadequately supported.
currentQuick:
Facial growth guidance appliances are orthodontic devices intended to influence how the jaws develop during childhood. The Biobloc is the system developed by John Mew in the orthotropics tradition, while the Twin Block is a functional appliance from mainstream orthodontics.
In looksmaxxing circles they are discussed as a way to shape the face while growth is still possible. Sources reviewed for this entry are thin, so the article is short.
How it works: According to Wikipedia, Mew's Biobloc approach uses a palate-expanding appliance followed by a postural appliance, based on the idea that oral posture shapes facial growth. Mainstream functional appliances such as the Twin Block are described in orthodontics as encouraging forward jaw posture during growth.
Risks and caveats: No source reviewed documents specific risks for these appliances. Wikipedia reports that Mike Mew, a promoter of the orthotropic approach, faced a misconduct hearing over harm to child patients. Orthodontic appliances generally need professional supervision.
deepLead:
Facial growth guidance appliances are orthodontic devices used in growing patients with the aim of directing jaw and facial development. The term is associated with orthotropics, the approach founded by John Mew, whose treatment system, the Biobloc, uses a palate-expanding appliance followed by a postural appliance .
Mew helped found the International Association of Facial Growth Guidance in 1987 . Mainstream orthodontic bodies say evidence for orthotropic efficacy is inadequate . The Twin Block, a different functional appliance from conventional orthodontics, is grouped with Biobloc in looksmaxxing discussion of growth appliances, although no source reviewed here describes it in detail.

name: Bimax / double jaw surgery

angle.text: Bimax surgery is the forum term for orthognathic surgery that moves both jaws, sought for a more defined profile and a corrected bite. The facial change is visible after healing, and the procedure has documented functional benefits.

summary: Forum shorthand for surgery that repositions both the upper and lower jaw at once; an established orthognathic procedure with documented functional benefits and real surgical risks.
note: Evidence is for bite and airway outcomes; recovery involves weeks of restrictions, and nerve numbness and infection are documented risks.
currentQuick:
Bimax, or double jaw surgery, means operating on both jaws in one procedure, typically a Le Fort I osteotomy of the upper jaw and a bilateral sagittal split osteotomy of the lower jaw. It is used for dentofacial deformities, bite problems, airway obstruction and facial disproportion.
Looksmaxxing communities treat it as a major hardmaxx option for changing facial structure. Surgeons usually combine it with orthodontic treatment before and after the operation.
How it works: The upper and lower jaw bones are cut and moved into new positions, then held with plates and screws while they heal. Wikipedia says infection rates up to 7% are reported and that nerve numbness is usually temporary.
Risks and caveats: Reported risks include bleeding, swelling, infection and facial numbness from nerve injury, which usually recovers within about three months but is rarely permanent. Full bone healing takes months, and diet is liquid for a time. Surgery is performed by oral and maxillofacial or plastic surgeons.
deepLead:
Bimaxillary or 'bimax' surgery is orthognathic surgery in which both jaws are repositioned together, commonly a Le Fort I osteotomy of the maxilla combined with a bilateral sagittal split osteotomy (BSSO) of the mandible . Wikipedia lists it among the main orthognathic procedures alongside genioplasty .
It is used to correct dentofacial deformities, malocclusion, jaw asymmetry and obstructive sleep apnea, usually after orthodontic preparation . In looksmaxxing culture the term is shorthand for the most comprehensive form of jaw surgery.

name: Genioplasty

angle.text: Genioplasty moves or reshapes the chin bone, or adds an implant, to improve chin projection and lower-face balance. The shape change is immediately visible, and forum posters discuss it as an alternative to double-jaw surgery.

summary: Chin bone surgery that moves or reshapes the chin; established oral surgery, discussed in forums as an alternative to double-jaw surgery.
note: Temporary or lasting lip and chin numbness is a documented complication.
currentQuick:
Genioplasty is surgery to change chin projection, height or width, usually by cutting and sliding the lower jaw border, or by adding an implant.
It is a long-established oral surgery procedure and a frequent topic on looksmax.org, where users weigh it against bimaxillary surgery.
How it works: In a sliding genioplasty a segment of the chin bone is cut, moved forward, back or vertically, and fixed with a titanium plate; implants add volume instead.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include swelling, temporary or lasting numbness of the lip and chin, infection and implant displacement. It is performed under general anaesthesia when bone is cut.
deepLead:
Genioplasty is chin surgery that changes the size, shape or projection of the chin. The term is used for operations that move or reshape the chin bone, most commonly a sliding genioplasty in which the lower border of the mandible is cut and repositioned, and it is also used more loosely for chin augmentation with implants. Surgeons who perform it include oral and maxillofacial surgeons, plastic surgeons and otolaryngologists.
In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as one of the more commonly considered facial bone procedures, often as an alternative or complement to double-jaw (bimaxillary) surgery for a recessed chin, and members debate how many millimetres of advancement to seek. The published literature consists mainly of surgical technique papers, accuracy studies of computer-planned surgery and registered trials of fixation and implant methods; no registry entry or study in this literature evaluates the looksmaxxing claims directly.
